title: The Fastest Punch in the Sea

pages.text: Pull back the rubber of a catapult and hold it. Nothing is moving, yet you can feel that something is ready to happen. The stretched rubber is storing energy. Let go, and that stored energy becomes movement in an instant. Energy stored in an object that has been stretched, squashed, or bent is called elastic potential energy. A drawn bow stores it. So does a squeezed spring, a trampoline, and the tight skin of a drum. One small animal has used the same trick for millions of years, and it does it better than any catapult.

pages.text: The peacock mantis shrimp lives on coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It is brightly coloured and only about as long as your hand. At the front of its body it carries two folded limbs that end in hard clubs. It uses them to smash open the shells of crabs and snails. The club swings out at about 23 metres per second, which is more than 80 km/h, and the whole strike is over in less than three thousandths of a second. The blow lands with a force of more than 700 newtons.
sentences: The peacock mantis shrimp lives on coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

At the front of its body it carries two folded limbs that end in hard clubs.
It uses them to smash open the shells of crabs and snails.
The club swings out at about 23 metres per second, which is more than 80 km/h, and the whole strike is over in less than three thousandths of a second.
The blow lands with a force of more than 700 newtons.
pages.alt: A brightly coloured mantis shrimp on a coral reef, with its two folded club-like front limbs clearly visible.

pages.text: Muscles alone could never move that fast. So the mantis shrimp does not use its muscles to punch. It uses them to load a spring. Part of its hard outer skeleton is shaped like a saddle. Slowly, the muscles bend this saddle, and a tiny latch holds it in place. Chemical energy from the animal’s food has been changed into elastic potential energy. Then the latch lets go. In an instant, the elastic potential energy becomes kinetic energy in the club. The energy is the same, but it is released in a far shorter time. That means far greater power.

pages.alt: A close-up diagram of the mantis shrimp’s striking limb showing the saddle-shaped spring bent and held by a small latch, then released.

pages.text: How strong is a 700-newton punch? To judge, we need the difference between mass and weight. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, measured in newtons. On Earth, each kilogram weighs about 10 newtons. A mantis shrimp with a mass of 50 grams, or 0.05 kilograms, weighs only 0.5 newtons. Its punch is therefore more than a thousand times its own weight. A person with a mass of 60 kilograms weighs 600 newtons. The shrimp’s punch is greater than that.

pages.text: There is more. The club moves so fast that the water behind it cannot keep up. The pressure there drops so low that the water turns to vapour, forming tiny bubbles. A moment later the bubbles collapse with a snap, giving off heat, sound, and even a flash of light. So the prey is hit twice: once by the club and once by the collapsing bubbles. Fishers who handle mantis shrimps with bare hands risk a split thumb, and large ones kept in tanks have been known to crack the glass.

pages.alt: The club of a mantis shrimp striking a crab shell under water, with a small burst of bubbles forming just behind the club.

pages.text: How does the club survive thousands of such blows without breaking? Under a microscope, it is built in layers, each one turned slightly from the one below, like a twisted pile of mats. A crack that starts cannot run straight through. Engineers are copying this pattern to make lighter, tougher helmets and aircraft parts. Designing with ideas borrowed from living things is called biomimicry. Relatives of the mantis shrimp live in the Gulf of Guinea too, and now and then one comes up in a fishing net. Nature tested these designs long before any laboratory did.

activities.question: Which of these is storing elastic potential energy?
options: A stone lying on the ground
A bow that has been drawn back

activities.question: What energy change happens when the mantis shrimp’s latch lets go?
options: Elastic potential energy changes into kinetic energy
Kinetic energy changes into chemical energy
Light energy changes into elastic potential energy

activities.question: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass is measured in newtons and weight in kilograms
Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on it

activities.question: Apply it: A hunter slowly draws a bow and then releases the arrow. Why does the arrow fly much faster than he could throw it by hand?
options: The bow adds extra energy that did not come from the hunter
The energy he stored slowly in the bow is released in a very short time
The arrow becomes lighter when it leaves the bow

activities.prompt: Arrange the steps of the mantis shrimp’s strike.
items: The shrimp takes in chemical energy from its food.
Its muscles slowly bend the saddle-shaped spring.
A latch holds the spring, storing elastic potential energy.
The latch releases, and the club swings out with kinetic energy.
Bubbles form behind the club and collapse, striking the prey again.

Kinetic energy: the energy an object has because it is moving.
